en: The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the King of Fragrances Bodhisattva, in one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śramaṇa Yijing.
Namo ratnatrayāya. Namo ārya-... [and so forth].

1. *Vajragarbhe* 2. *bodhisattva* 3. *mahāsattva* 4. *namo gandharvarājāya* 5. *bodhisattva* 6. *mahāsattva* 7. *ijji* 8. *mijji* 9. *hanti* 10. *mandi* 11. *sarvāṭa* 12. *santani* 13. *kāliṣapaṇa* 14. *dipame* 15. *paridyaccha* 16. *svāhā* This is the dhāraṇī first.
One must recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times with a sincere mind.
Then, before an image of Avalokiteśvara,
construct a square altar measuring four cubits on each side.
Offer fragrant incense, such as flowers and the like.
At night, burn a lamp with purified cow ghee,
ensuring that the light does not go out.
At midnight, the mantra practitioner must arise.
Donning clean garments and properly adorning himself,
he should recite this dhāraṇī one thousand and eight times before the image.
At dawn, one must finish [the ritual] and may not fall into昏睡 (torpor).
On that day, there will be those who send the mantra-practitioner wealth and other offerings;
furthermore, if one seeks to accomplish some other great matter, [one should proceed accordingly].
One must paint the Bodhisattva Gandharvarāja upon a silk cloth; the painter must not eat past midday and must observe the eight precepts of the fast.
As for the method of painting the image, its dimensions may be made as large or small as desired.
The flesh of his body is entirely white, his facial features are upright and handsome, he wears a celestial crown upon his head, and a jeweled necklace adorns his neck.
His right arm hangs down with all five fingers extended, forming the mudrā of bestowing fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*).
From the tips of his five fingers, he rains down nectar as an offering to sentient beings in the five realms of existence.
Beneath his hands, paint three or five black spirits.
His left arm is bent at the elbow, with the hand placed against his left breast.
He holds a lotus flower.
That flower emerges from the lotus beneath his feet; the flower is white and red, and the lotus beneath his feet is likewise white and red.
The nape of his neck and back were surrounded by a halo,
above which was a parasol;
he wore garments made of five-colored brocades and silks.
Two strands of beads, one red and one yellow, are draped over the shoulders;
this image must be completed on that very day.
One must not use leather or glue.
Before the image, burn incense and recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while fasting for one day and one night.
First, one must prepare a large square altar in water.
Then, using sandalwood, grind it to create eight small square altars, each twelve finger-widths in size;
first, prepare three of these altars.
One portion is used for making offerings to the Buddha;
one portion is used for making offerings to the Dharma;
and one portion is used for making offerings to the Sangha.
On the fourth altar, one makes offerings to Amitābha Buddha;
on the fifth, to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva;
and on the sixth, to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva.
Seventh, they made offerings to the Bodhisattva King of Incense;
eighth, they made offerings to all the various benevolent deities and others,
each taking fine, pure food, fruits, incense, and flowers.
It is arranged on all four sides.
As for the ritual, it may be performed on either the fourteenth or the fifteenth day of any month.
One should then take one thousand and eight stalks of *jāti* flowers—these are called *karpūra* flowers in Chinese.
Recite it once and cast it upon the chest of the image.
After performing this rite, one must rise every midnight;
one should constantly recite it one thousand and eight times before the image.
When someone comes to offer wealth and property,
one must not accumulate it out of stinginess or greed; rather,
it must immediately be used for one's own needs and given as alms to the poor and destitute.
This is the dharma of the Bodhisattva Gandharāja.
Furthermore, there is another essential abbreviated practice:
the method for upholding the mantra.
The practitioner shall bathe, don new and clean robes,
observe the eightfold precepts,
and establish the purity of the site exactly according to the ritual of the altar.
Arrange the offerings in successive order, scattering flowers, burning incense,
and lighting lamps. Beginning at midnight,
sit upright within the maṇḍala.
Recite the mantra one thousand and eight times, using one thousand and eight stalks of *campaka* flowers.
With each recitation of the mantra, cast one flower onto the body of the Bodhisattva.
When reciting the mantra,
one must not hear the sound of birds chirping;
one should break the fast with the "three white foods."
Burn安息香 (an-xi-xiang, *agaru*) as an offering.
Each day, bathe with filtered water and fragrant decoctions,
and wear separate, clean garments.
Before entering or leaving the altar, one must wash and purify oneself both large and small.
At dawn and at midnight, when entering the altar, one must chew a willow branch.
Only then may one enter the altar and recite the mantra with single-minded concentration.
Do not contemplate external phenomena; then you will see divine efficacy and radiance.
Upon seeing this efficacy, cease [contemplation].
Even when the light is not seen, there is still the sign of movement.
Wherever one practices, one will obtain great rewards.
Regarding the method of upholding the mantra, one must not violate the precepts.
Furthermore, one must not come into physical contact with a woman; should one touch a woman, there will be no efficacy.
The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Gandharāja (King of Fragrance)
